I have farmed these two mu in Quzhou for 45 years, and at 68 I know every patch of this soil. With only my wife and me in the household, I keep my plan simple, labor-efficient, and grounded in what actually works on this small plot. I will sow hybrid spring maize in late May because hybrid seed gives yields that traditional varieties simply cannot match, and after decades of comparing them I see no reason to change. I will apply about 15 kg of nitrogen per mu—half as basal compound fertilizer and half as urea topdressed at the jointing stage—plus roughly 5 kg of phosphorus and 4 kg of potassium per mu at sowing. That is enough for this land; over-fertilizing wastes money and does not help the crop. Because I have well irrigation, I will water three times: right after sowing to secure germination, once at the big trumpet stage when the summer heat hits, and once during grain filling if the weather turns dry. For crop protection, I will spray herbicide once when the maize is still small, and one round of insecticide if I see corn borer damage; on two mu I can walk the field and spot problems early, so two applications are sufficient. I will use rotary tillage to prepare the seedbed—it is less backbreaking than ploughing and gives the fine soil contact I need for good emergence. In a normal year I expect about 550 kg per mu, which will cover our household grain needs and leave some surplus to sell.
